# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 1.750 mediaeval settlements, walled oases, fortified citadels, riverine ports and caravan staging posts active across Central Asia between the Mongol invasion of 1219AD and the late Timurid era in 1500AD (encompassing 3.890.946 km² across eight territorial units). Synthesising regional archaeological excavation inventories, the University College London Central Asian Archaeological Landscapes (UCL CAAL) database, Al-Thurayya Islamic historical gazetteers and national cultural heritage registers [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Stephen2012Deep; @Zali2022Necessity; @Sadigov2024Internatio; @Laruelle2021Central; @Anon2024Ultrasound], the compendium captures the structural transformation of the Central Asian urban hierarchy under Mongol, Chagatai, Ulus Jochi and Timurid rule. The catalogued entries are led by the grand imperial metropolises of Transoxiana, headed by Samarkand (115.000 peak residents under Timur) and Bukhara (75.000 residents), the resilient delta capital of Kunya-Urgench (55.000 residents in 1350AD), the strategic commercial transit hubs of Tashkent (42.000 residents) and Shahrisabz (38.000 residents), the lower Ural River emporium of Saraishyk (32.000 residents in 1350AD) and key fortified frontier nodes along the Syr Darya corridor led by Sighnaq (30.000 residents), Andijan (28.000 residents), Akhsikent (28.000 residents), Khujand (26.000 residents), Qarshi (26.000 residents), Otrar (25.000 residents), Turkistan (Yasi) (22.000 residents) and Sauran (22.000 residents). Across all 1.750 catalogued nodes, the register documents occupational sequences, geographic coordinates and territorial assignments. Alongside the included settlements, the source ledger accounts for 3.326 excluded candidate entities out of 5.076 total evaluated entries without discrepancy.

# Background

Mediaeval settlement systems across Central Asia underwent profound morphological and functional reorganisations between 1219AD and 1500AD [@Stephen2012Deep; @Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Zali2022Necessity]. Prior to the Mongol invasion, urban life was organized around the classical tripartite Islamic urban model: a fortified central citadel (*ark* or *kuhandiz*), an inner walled city (*shahristan*) and extensive commercial and artisanal suburbs (*rabad*) enclosed by outer earthen ramparts [@Zali2022Necessity; @Tretyakov2024Factors]. Major oasis centers such as Samarkand (Afrasiyab), Bukhara, Gurganj and Merv sustained extensive domestic craft quarters, textile workshops and international trading caravanserais [@Stephen2012Deep; @Tretyakov2024Factors].

The military shock of the 1219-1221AD Mongol campaigns radically disrupted this urban geography [@Stephen2012Deep; @Amlashi2025Consequenc]. At sites such as Afrasiyab (the ancient core of Samarkand) and Merv, comprehensive destruction of aqueducts and walls forced permanent shifts in settlement topography: when Samarkand revived under Chagatai and Timurid governance, habitation relocated south of the ruined Afrasiyab plateau onto the modern city site, while Merv shifted toward the new Timurid walled sector of Abdullah Khan Kala [@Stephen2012Deep; @Zali2022Necessity].

In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, urbanization bifurcated along dual functional lines [@Laruelle2021Central; @Balabanlilar2007Lords]:
First, in the sedentary river oases of Transoxiana, the Timurid state executed ambitious royal building programmes, creating monumental congregational mosques, madrasas, covered market halls and royal suburban palace-gardens characterized by glazed ceramic tile revetments and double-shelled turquoise domes [@Anon2024Features; @Dmitriy2024Ultrathin; @Zubkova2024Integratio].
Second, along the northern ecological boundary between irrigated agriculture and the Kipchak steppe, fortified frontier towns such as Sighnaq, Sauran, Otrar and Saraishyk flourished as active trade entrepôts where pastoral nomads exchanged horses, sheep, hides and wool for textiles, grain, manufactured metal wares and luxury craft goods [@Laruelle2021Central; @Akhmetkul2025History; @Sadigov2024Internatio].

# Methodology

Settlement records were compiled by cross-referencing national heritage registries across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan with international digital gazetteers [@Sadigov2024Internatio; @Laruelle2021Central; @Anon2024Ultrasound]. Every catalogued settlement entry carries standard WGS84 geographic coordinates, an administrative territorial assignment to one of the eight regional units, a documented longitudinal population time-series across active benchmark years and citation references to primary archaeological and historical surveys [@Balabanlilar2007Lords; @Stephen2012Deep].

Candidate entities were systematically audited against spatial and chronological criteria in the regional source ledger [@Anon2024Ultrasound]. Out of 5.076 total evaluated candidates, 1.750 entities were confirmed as active domestic settlements or fortified nodes within the 1219-1500AD temporal window and regional bounding mask. A total of 3.326 candidate records were excluded: 2.148 records represented settlements lacking active occupation within the study period or situated outside the geographic mask, while 1.178 records constituted duplicate archaeological aliases, variant phonetic transliterations, or minor isolated monument find-spots situated within 5 km of documented primary urban centers [@Anon2024Ultrasound].

# Testing and Validation

Reconciliation of the source ledger confirms 1.750 included settlement entities and 3.326 excluded candidate records, accounting for all 5.076 evaluated entities with zero unaccounted discrepancies. Every catalogued settlement possesses geocoded coordinates within its designated regional mask. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} illustrates the rank-size distribution and leading urban nodes across Central Asia under Mongol and Timurid rule.

## Sub-Regional Settlement Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-mongol} summarizes the spatial distribution of catalogued mediaeval settlements across the eight analytical territories alongside their respective leading urban centers. The Syr Darya frontier towns lead the domain with 386 catalogued sites, reflecting intensive fortification and trade infrastructure along the Jaxartes river valley, followed by Ferghana and Tashkent (332 sites) and the Timurid Mawarannahr core (310 sites). Table \ref{tab:excluded-mongol} reports the leading 30 of 3.326 excluded candidate entities in the regional source ledger.

## Archaeological Caveats and Taphonomic Preservation

Three taphonomic and spatial preservation dynamics condition mediaeval settlement analysis in this gazetteer [@Anon2024Ultrasound; @Laruelle2021Central; @Stephen2012Deep]:

First, mudbrick and adobe structural degradation poses significant challenges to architectural volume reconstruction [@Anon2024Ultrasound; @Zali2022Necessity]. In desert and semi-arid environments (such as the Kyzylkum, Karakum and Betpak-Dala margins), unbaked loess bricks and earthen pisé walls erode into smooth mounds (*tepas*) unless protected by fired-brick revetments, obscuring domestic house plans beneath meters of collapsed architectural debris [@Anon2024Ultrasound].

Second, intensive post-mediaeval urban continuity has obliterated mediaeval settlement strata in thriving modern cities [@Zali2022Necessity; @Tretyakov2024Factors]. In metropolises such as Tashkent, Bukhara, Samarkand and Khujand, modern multi-story construction and infrastructure development have built over mediaeval residential quarters, limiting systematic archaeological access to rescue excavation trenches and protected historical monument precincts [@Zali2022Necessity]. Conversely, ruined deserted cities such as Sauran, Otrar and Kunya-Urgench retain pristine street layouts, water reservoirs (*hauz*) and fortification networks amenable to high-resolution satellite remote sensing [@Anon2024Ultrasound].

Third, hydrological instability and river course shifts have transformed settlement distributions across deltaic environments [@Ibragimov2024Talk; @Sadigov2024Internatio]. In Khwarazm, periodic shifts in the main discharge channels of the lower Amu Darya (such as the dried-up Daryalyk and Daudan channels) caused sudden abandonment of extensive irrigation oases and fortified agricultural settlements, leaving hundreds of intact *qalas* marooned in hyper-arid sand plains far from modern active water sources [@Ibragimov2024Talk; @Sadigov2024Internatio].
